prize_parts.citation: for showing how technology and trade shape labour demand, wages and the distribution of earnings

statement.case_for: I ranked B018 first in my opening and have moved B027 to the top after reading colleagues' attribution arguments. I am not moving because of support counts. The scientific case stands on its own. The task framework, the skills-versus-technology literature and the local labour-market evidence on import competition together changed how economists and policymakers understand who gains and loses from technology and trade. The designs are transparent and have been replicated, extended and challenged for years, so the main findings have been tested. The work is cross-disciplinary and moves from theory to measurement to policy, which is the kind of contribution I value. Attribution is more tractable here than in B018: Autor links the task and trade-shock strands, Hanson anchors the trade-shock evidence, and Katz anchors the long-run demand-and-supply-of-skills literature. That makes a three-name award with a coherent citation workable, which is not true of choosing three from eight names in the New Keynesian field.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the cost of the three-name cap. Dorn is a core co-author of the China-shock papers and is excluded, and the task framework has other contributors, including Acemoglu, who received the 2024 prize. The magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated. A citation covering both technology and trade may also read as two prizes combined rather than one discovery. If the committee judges that the New Keynesian framework is more fundamental to the discipline, B018 has greater policy reach, but its attribution problem is much worse.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B027 first but proposes Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He argues the China-shock work is most cleanly credited to that trio and that the task framework has wider authorship that includes Katz.
responses.response: I agree the China-shock papers are most cleanly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and I take the loss of Dorn seriously. But a trio built around the trade-shock papers would credit only the narrower empirical strand and drop the skills-versus-technology literature on which the broader citation depends. Katz anchors the long-run evidence on skill demand and supply, and that is what lets the citation cover technology and trade together. I would accept your configuration if the committee prefers a trade-adjustment citation, but I think it describes a different and narrower achievement.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B027 first. She notes the transparent designs and the replication work, and she flags overlap with Acemoglu's task-based work and with the 2024 and 2025 prizes as well as the three-name limit.
responses.response: I share both the endorsement and the caveat. The Acemoglu overlap is a real attribution complication, but the 2024 prize was framed around institutions and prosperity, not around labour-demand measurement. The citation I propose rests on the empirical record on wages, tasks and trade exposure, so I think overlap can be managed through the wording. Your point about replication scrutiny is the reason I put the maturity of this body of work above that of the newer mobility and household-debt candidates.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first and proposes Kiyotaki and Moore alone. He argues that Gertler and Gilchrist belong to a financial-accelerator strand that overlaps with the 2022 prize, and that the collateral-amplification mechanism is a foundational building block of macro-finance.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators and that the 2022 overlap argues for a two-person award, which is cleaner than my own three-name proposal that included Gertler. I would keep B006 as a serious alternative. My reservation is that the model is mainly theoretical and its direct empirical identification is thinner than the labour-market evidence in B027. That is a difference in the strength of confirmation, not a judgment that your candidate is less important.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B012 first and proposes Helpman and Melitz. He argues that firm heterogeneity moved trade analysis from industries to firms and gave a tractable account of the gains from trade, building on the Krugman prize.
responses.response: I rank B012 sixth, and I recognise that Melitz is the clear originator and that the framework is mature. I put it below B027 for two reasons. Krugman's 2008 prize covers adjacent ground, and the credit around Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is unsettled. B027 has fewer unresolved attribution questions and a broader evidentiary base. If the committee chose B012 I would find a Helpman and Melitz award defensible.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers Katz or Dorn as the third name, which depends on whether the citation covers both technology and trade or only the trade-shock strand.
How much the overlap with Acemoglu's task-based work and the 2024 prize should reduce the claim.
The long-run size and persistence of the China-shock effects, which are still debated.
Whether two strands should be treated as one achievement or two separate ones.
Whether the attribution difficulty in B018 can be resolved through a narrower citation, since I have not found a clean three-name solution.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the proposed laureates Autor, Hanson and Katz, or for the alternatives. My profile lists co-authors on refugee matching, kidney exchange and Lund work, and none of them is credited in the shortlisted candidates. My SSE affiliation and COVID-policy co-authorship with SSE economists are institutional ties to colleagues, not connections to any candidate.
